units.translation: Being just, he will not be unhappy.
which generally means to wail or lament, sometimes is said of a joyful shout: see Thes. vol. 1, 2 p. 832.
I cried aloud long ago for joy.
a mode which is no mode, not to be sung
and about yourself you utter a lawless strain.
Another example of this verb is Eur. Hel. 371.
Why did you wail these things about Loxias?
For are you not a child, and even more senseless than this one?

[unwounded. Explained by Hesychius from Aeschylus' Lycurgus as ἄτρωτος ἐκ χειρός [unwounded by hand], which seems to be referred to the gloss that has fallen out ἀν' οὓς ἔχων: ἄνω τὸ οὓς ἔχων [having the ears upward], as said at fr. 125.]

Schol. ἐναντία φαίνεται τὰ θεῶν, οἷον ἀντικειμένους ἡμῖν ὁρῶ τοὺς θεούς [the things of the gods appear opposite, as if I see the gods opposed to us]. In M' ἐν ὄμμασι τ᾽ ἀνταῖα [and hostile in the eyes] (i.e., τἀνταΐα [the hostile things]), whence in some copies ὄμμασί τ᾿ ἀνταῖα [and hostile in the eyes].
For to me now all things are full of fear, and the hostile things of the gods appear in my eyes.
ἀνταία [hostile]: opposite, suppliant. Aeschylus in Semele (fr. 236).
the things of the gods appear opposite, as if I see the gods opposed to us
to raise a war-cry in answer
and at once the echo of the island rock raised a shrill cry in answer.
Thus from the copy, for ἐξημείψατο [he exchanged], which is in M.
the tyrant of the gods has repaid me with these evil punishments.
having suffered evil, he repaid with evils.
How is it not right to repay an enemy with evils?
I meet with something, I fall in with something.
having met with the wild sea.
having met the Argive expedition (ἀνστήσας M in text).
[saying that he killed in the same manner in return.]
and I have nothing to say against.
but I will no longer speak against the gods about dying.
struck by the desire of those who love in return.
I resist, I withstand an attack.
at first the stream of the Persian army held out.
In the manuscripts of other writers sometimes ἀνθήλιος [facing the sun] is written contrary to the rule of the grammarians, about which see Lobeck on Soph. Ai. p. 295 of the third edition.
and august seats and gods facing the sun.
who is in place of a man.
a tearful grain of dust in place of a man.
I advise sending wise and good men as adversaries against him.
